note: Synthetic sample material written for CourseLab testing. It is not actual University of Florida course content. Questions were written by hand against the synthetic fixtures; numeric answers are recomputed by the worker when the sample is loaded.

course.name: Sample course: QMB 3250-like (synthetic)
course.goal: Try CourseLab with synthetic material before importing your own.

note.summary: Simple regression fits a straight line that makes the squared prediction misses as small as possible. Each miss is a residual.

points.text: A residual is what the line got wrong for one observation: observed minus predicted.
points.quote: A residual is the observed value minus the predicted value

points.text: The fitted line goes through the point of means, and its residuals add up to zero.
points.quote: The least-squares line always passes through the point of means

note.summary: The slope is an average change per one-unit increase in x. The intercept is the prediction at x = 0 and often has no practical meaning.

points.text: Say the slope as an average change in the response per unit of x, in context and with units.
points.quote: The slope b1 is the estimated change in the average response for a one-unit increase in x

points.text: Only interpret the intercept when x = 0 is inside or near the observed data.
points.quote: It has a practical meaning only when x = 0 lies inside, or close to, the range of the observed data

points.text: Predictions far outside the observed x range are extrapolation.
points.quote: Predicting far outside the observed range of x is called extrapolation and is unreliable

note.summary: R-squared is the share of variation explained; RMSE is the typical miss in the units of the response.

points.text: R-squared = 1 − SSE/SST, the proportion of variation in y explained by the regression.
points.quote: R-squared is the proportion of the variation in y that is explained by the regression

points.text: In simple regression RMSE divides SSE by n − 2 before taking the square root.
points.quote: In simple regression RMSE = square root of SSE/(n - 2)

topics.name: Testing a slope: t ratio and p-value

note.summary: The t ratio compares an estimate with its standard error; the p-value says how surprising that ratio would be if the true slope were zero.

points.text: t ratio = estimate ÷ standard error.
points.quote: t = b1 divided by the standard error of b1

points.text: A p-value is computed assuming the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the null is true.
points.quote: A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true

points.text: A 95% interval that excludes zero means significance at the 5% level.
points.quote: If the interval does not contain zero, the slope is significant at the 5% level

note.summary: In multiple regression each coefficient holds the other predictors fixed, and adjusted R-squared corrects R-squared for model size.

points.text: A partial slope is a change per unit of one predictor with the others held fixed.
points.quote: holding the other predictors in the model fixed

points.text: Plain R-squared cannot fall when predictors are added, so it cannot rank models of different sizes.
points.quote: R-squared never decreases when a predictor is added, even a useless one

points.text: Adjusted R-squared applies a penalty for the number of predictors k.
points.quote: adjusted R-squared = 1 - (1 - R-squared)(n - 1)/(n - k - 1)

note.summary: The F test judges the model as a whole. Multicollinearity makes individual coefficients unstable even when the whole model predicts well.

points.text: The F test's null hypothesis is that every slope is zero.
points.quote: The null hypothesis is that all k slope coefficients are zero

points.text: Correlated predictors inflate standard errors.
points.quote: It inflates the standard errors of the affected coefficients

points.text: A VIF above 10 is a common warning sign.
points.quote: A common rule of thumb treats a VIF above 10 as a sign of serious multicollinearity

note.summary: Criteria such as adjusted R-squared, AIC and BIC trade fit against complexity.

points.text: Lower AIC and BIC are better; higher adjusted R-squared is better.
points.quote: For AIC and BIC, smaller is better

points.text: BIC's penalty is heavier, so it favors smaller models.
points.quote: BIC penalizes extra predictors more heavily than AIC and tends to choose smaller models

points.text: Stepwise searches overstate significance.
points.quote: the reported p-values of the final model are too optimistic

note.summary: Indicator (dummy) variables code categories as 0/1 and compare each category with a baseline.

points.text: c categories need c − 1 indicators.
points.quote: A categorical variable with c categories needs c - 1 indicator variables

points.text: The category without an indicator is the baseline.
points.quote: The category that receives no indicator is the baseline category

points.text: An indicator coefficient is a difference from the baseline, other predictors fixed.
points.quote: the estimated difference in the average response between that category and the baseline category

note.summary: An interaction lets one predictor's slope depend on another predictor.

points.text: With an indicator d, the slope of x is b1 for d = 0 and b1 + b3 for d = 1.
points.quote: the slope of x is b1 when d = 0 and b1 + b3 when d = 1

points.text: In the sample model the advertising slope rises from 2.479 to 3.471 during a promotion.
points.quote: With a promotion the slope of ad_spend is 2.479 + 0.992 = 3.471

points.text: Keep main effects when their interaction is in the model.
points.quote: Keep the main effects in the model whenever their interaction is included

note.summary: Both methods smooth out noise; they differ in how much weight recent observations get.

points.text: A moving average is the mean of the last k observations.
points.quote: A moving-average forecast for the next period is the mean of the most recent k observations

points.text: Exponential smoothing blends the latest actual with the previous forecast.
points.quote: F(t+1) = alpha Y(t) + (1 - alpha) F(t)

points.text: Large alpha reacts fast; small alpha is smooth.
points.quote: A value of alpha close to 1 puts most of the weight on the latest observation

note.summary: MAD, MSE and MAPE summarize forecast errors; seasonal indexes adjust a trend forecast for the time of year.

points.text: MAD averages the absolute errors.
points.quote: MAD, the mean absolute deviation, is the average of the absolute errors

points.text: MAPE is unit-free, so it compares across series.
points.quote: so it can be compared across series with different units

points.text: A multiplicative seasonal forecast is trend × index.
points.quote: the forecast is the trend value multiplied by the seasonal index for that season

questions.stem: A fitted line is y-hat = 5 + 2x. One observation has x = 10 and y = 28. What is the residual for this observation?
questions.hint: Residual = observed − predicted. Find the prediction first.
questions.explanation: The prediction is 5 + 2(10) = 25, so the residual is 28 − 25 = 3. A positive residual means the point lies above the line. Subtracting in the other order (−3) is the most common slip.

cite.quote: A residual is the observed value minus the predicted value

questions.stem: Why does the least-squares method square the residuals before adding them up?
choices: So positive and negative misses do not cancel, and large misses count more
Because squared residuals always add up to zero
So that the fitted line passes through every data point
To convert the residuals into the units of x
questions.hint: Think about what would happen if you simply added raw residuals.
questions.explanation: Raw residuals from a least-squares line sum to zero, so they cannot measure fit. Squaring removes the signs and penalizes large misses more heavily. The line does not pass through every point, and squaring does not change units to those of x.

cite.quote: Squaring keeps positive and negative misses from cancelling and penalizes large misses more heavily

questions.stem: A least-squares line is fitted to data with mean x = 12 and mean y = 40. Which statement must be true?
choices: The line predicts y = 40 when x = 12
The intercept of the line equals 40
Half of the observations lie exactly on the line
The largest residual occurs at x = 12
questions.hint: There is one point every least-squares line is guaranteed to pass through.
questions.explanation: The least-squares line always passes through the point of means, so at x = 12 it predicts 40. Nothing forces the intercept to equal the mean of y or any observation to sit on the line.

cite.quote: The least-squares line always passes through the point of means

questions.stem: Weekly sales (thousand dollars) were regressed on advertising spend (thousand dollars), giving sales-hat = 12.823 + 2.989 ad_spend. What is the best interpretation of 2.989?
choices: Each additional thousand dollars of advertising is associated with about 2.989 thousand dollars more weekly sales, on average
Advertising causes sales to rise by exactly 2.989 thousand dollars in every store
Weekly sales are 2.989 thousand dollars when nothing is spent on advertising
About 2.989% of the variation in sales is explained by advertising
questions.hint: A slope is an average change in y per one-unit change in x.
questions.explanation: The slope is the estimated change in average sales for a one-unit (thousand-dollar) increase in advertising. It describes an association, not a guaranteed causal effect for every store. Sales at zero advertising is the intercept, and the share of variation explained is R-squared.

cite.quote: The slope b1 is the estimated change in the average response for a one-unit increase in x

questions.stem: Using sales-hat = 12.823 + 2.989 ad_spend (both in thousand dollars), predict weekly sales for a store that spends 20 thousand dollars on advertising. Give the answer in thousand dollars.
questions.hint: Substitute 20 for ad_spend.

cite.quote: The fitted line is sales-hat = 12.823 + 2.989 ad_spend

questions.stem: In the store-sales data, advertising spend ranges from about 5 to 30 thousand dollars. An analyst uses the fitted line to predict sales for a store spending 90 thousand dollars. What is the main concern?
choices: It is extrapolation: the linear pattern may not hold far outside the observed range
The slope must be re-estimated because 90 is an even number
The prediction is invalid because the intercept is positive
R-squared becomes negative for large values of x
questions.hint: Compare 90 with the range of x values used to fit the line.
questions.explanation: Predicting far outside the observed range of x is extrapolation and is unreliable, because the data say nothing about how sales behave there. The sign of the intercept and the value of R-squared are not the issue.

cite.quote: Predicting far outside the observed range of x is called extrapolation and is unreliable

questions.stem: A simple regression has SSE = 17,133 and SST = 44,525. Compute R-squared (as a proportion, to three decimals).
questions.hint: R-squared = 1 − SSE/SST.
questions.explanation: R-squared = 1 − 17,133/44,525 = 1 − 0.3848 = 0.615. About 61.5% of the variation in sales is explained by advertising. Reporting SSE/SST (0.385) is the unexplained share, not R-squared.

cite.quote: R-squared is the proportion of the variation in y that is explained by the regression

questions.stem: A simple regression on n = 60 stores has SSE = 17,133. Compute the root mean square error (RMSE).
questions.hint: Divide SSE by n − 2, then take the square root.
questions.explanation: RMSE = sqrt(17,133/58) = sqrt(295.4) ≈ 17.19. A typical prediction misses by about 17 thousand dollars. Dividing by n instead of n − 2 gives a slightly smaller, incorrect value.

cite.quote: In simple regression RMSE = square root of SSE/(n - 2)

questions.stem: A regression of sales on advertising has R-squared = 0.62. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: About 62% of the variation in sales is explained by the linear relationship with advertising
The linear model is appropriate because R-squared is above 0.5
62% of the predictions are exactly correct
The correlation between sales and advertising is 0.62
questions.hint: R-squared is a proportion of variation; it does not check assumptions.
questions.explanation: R-squared is the proportion of variation in y explained by the regression. It does not show the model is appropriate — a residual plot is needed for that — and in simple regression the correlation is the square root of R-squared (about 0.79), not R-squared itself.

cite.quote: A high R-squared does not show that the model is appropriate; always look at a residual plot

questions.stem: A slope estimate is 2.989 with standard error 0.310. Compute the t ratio for testing whether the slope is zero.
questions.hint: t ratio = estimate ÷ standard error.
questions.explanation: t = 2.989/0.310 ≈ 9.64. A ratio this far from zero gives a tiny p-value, so the slope is clearly different from zero.

cite.quote: t = b1 divided by the standard error of b1
The t ratio is simply the estimate divided by its standard error

questions.stem: The test of a slope gives a p-value of 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: If the true slope were zero, a t ratio at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
There is a 3% probability that the true slope is zero
There is a 97% probability that the model is correct
The slope explains 3% of the variation in the response
questions.hint: A p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true.
questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, computed assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis (or the model) is true, and it is unrelated to variation explained.

cite.quote: A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true

questions.stem: A slope estimate is 2.989 with standard error 0.310, from a simple regression with n = 60. The critical t value for 95% confidence with 58 degrees of freedom is 2.002. Compute the lower limit of the 95% confidence interval for the slope.
questions.hint: Estimate minus (critical t × standard error).
questions.explanation: Lower limit = 2.989 − 2.002(0.310) = 2.989 − 0.621 = 2.368. The whole interval (2.368 to 3.610) is above zero, so the slope is significant at the 5% level.

cite.quote: If the interval does not contain zero, the slope is significant at the 5% level

questions.stem: In a model predicting weekly sales from ad_spend, price and promo, the coefficient of price is −2.998. What does it mean?
choices: Among stores with the same advertising and promotion status, a one-dollar higher price is associated with about 2.998 thousand dollars lower average sales
Raising price by one dollar lowers sales by 2.998 thousand dollars regardless of what else changes
Price explains 2.998% of the variation in sales
Stores with higher prices spend 2.998 thousand dollars less on advertising
questions.hint: What is being held fixed in a multiple regression coefficient?
questions.explanation: Each coefficient in a multiple regression is a partial slope: the change in average response per unit of that predictor, holding the other predictors in the model fixed. It says nothing about situations where the other predictors change too.

cite.quote: holding the other predictors in the model fixed

questions.stem: A model with k = 4 predictors fitted to n = 60 stores has R-squared = 0.9602. Compute adjusted R-squared (to four decimals).
questions.explanation: Adjusted R² = 1 − (0.0398)(59)/55 = 1 − 0.0427 = 0.9573, matching the 'RSquare Adj' line of the output. It is slightly below R² because of the penalty for four predictors.

cite.quote: adjusted R-squared = 1 - (1 - R-squared)(n - 1)/(n - k - 1)
RSquare Adj 0.9573

questions.stem: A weak predictor is added to a regression. R-squared rises from 0.810 to 0.812, but adjusted R-squared falls from 0.801 to 0.799. What is the best reading?
choices: The new predictor improves the fit by less than would be expected by chance, so the smaller model is preferable on this criterion
The larger model is better because R-squared increased
There must be a calculation error, because the two measures always move together
The new predictor is causing multicollinearity
questions.hint: Which of the two measures can never go down when a variable is added?
questions.explanation: R-squared never decreases when a predictor is added, so its increase is uninformative. Adjusted R-squared rises only when the improvement exceeds what chance would give; a drop favors the smaller model. The two measures can and do move in opposite directions.

cite.quote: R-squared never decreases when a predictor is added, even a useless one

questions.stem: A regression with four predictors reports an F ratio of 332.04 with Prob > F below 0.0001. What can be concluded?
choices: At least one of the four predictors is useful for predicting the response
All four predictors are individually significant
The model explains more than 99.99% of the variation
The residuals are normally distributed
questions.hint: State the null hypothesis of the overall F test, then negate it.
questions.explanation: The F test's null hypothesis is that all slope coefficients are zero. Rejecting it shows at least one predictor is useful — not that every one is; individual t ratios address that. It says nothing about normality.

cite.quote: It does not show that every predictor is useful

questions.stem: A regression with k = 4 predictors and n = 60 observations has R-squared = 0.9602. Compute the overall F ratio (to the nearest whole number is fine).
questions.explanation: F = (0.9602/4)/(0.0398/55) = 0.24005/0.000724 ≈ 331.7, in line with the F Ratio in the output (the small difference comes from rounding R²).

cite.quote: The F ratio is the model mean square divided by the error mean square

questions.stem: Two predictors in a model are very strongly correlated with each other. The overall F test is highly significant, yet neither predictor's t ratio is significant. What explains this?
choices: Multicollinearity has inflated the standard errors of the two coefficients
The sample size is too large
The response variable is not normally distributed
The model has too few predictors
questions.hint: What happens to standard errors when predictors carry overlapping information?
questions.explanation: Multicollinearity inflates the standard errors of the affected coefficients, shrinking their t ratios, while the model as a whole can still predict well — hence a significant F with insignificant individual tests.

cite.quote: It inflates the standard errors of the affected coefficients

questions.stem: When one predictor is regressed on the other predictors in the model, the R-squared is 0.92. Compute that predictor's variance inflation factor (VIF).
questions.hint: VIF = 1/(1 − R² of that predictor on the others).
questions.explanation: VIF = 1/(1 − 0.92) = 1/0.08 = 12.5. That is above the common rule-of-thumb threshold of 10, signalling serious multicollinearity.

cite.quote: A common rule of thumb treats a VIF above 10 as a sign of serious multicollinearity

questions.stem: Three candidate models are compared. Which rule matches how the criteria are used?
choices: Prefer the highest adjusted R-squared and the lowest AIC or BIC
Prefer the highest value of every criterion
Prefer the lowest adjusted R-squared and the highest AIC
Prefer the model with the most predictors when criteria disagree
questions.hint: Fit measures are 'higher is better'; information criteria are penalties.
questions.explanation: For adjusted R-squared larger is better; for AIC and BIC smaller is better.

cite.quote: For AIC and BIC, smaller is better

questions.stem: With n = 60 observations, AIC picks a five-predictor model while BIC picks a three-predictor model. Why can this happen?
choices: BIC's penalty per parameter, ln(n), is larger than AIC's penalty of 2, so BIC favors smaller models
AIC ignores the sum of squared errors
BIC can only be used with fewer than four predictors
One of the two criteria must have been computed incorrectly
questions.hint: Compare ln(60) with 2.
questions.explanation: Both criteria start from n ln(SSE/n) but AIC adds 2 per parameter and BIC adds ln(n) per parameter. Since ln(60) ≈ 4.09 > 2, BIC penalizes extra predictors more heavily and tends to choose smaller models.

cite.quote: BIC penalizes extra predictors more heavily than AIC and tends to choose smaller models

questions.stem: Using AIC = n ln(SSE/n) + 2(k + 1), compute AIC for a model with n = 60, k = 4 and SSE = 1770.53 (to one decimal).
questions.hint: Compute SSE/n first, take the natural log, multiply by n, then add 2(k + 1).

cite.quote: AIC can be computed (up to a constant) as n ln(SSE/n) + 2(k + 1)

questions.stem: A region variable has four categories: North, South, East and West. How many indicator variables should be included in a regression that has an intercept?
questions.hint: One category must serve as the baseline.
questions.explanation: A categorical variable with c categories needs c − 1 indicators, so 4 − 1 = 3. Including all four together with the intercept creates perfect multicollinearity (the dummy variable trap).

cite.quote: A categorical variable with c categories needs c - 1 indicator variables

questions.stem: In a model without interaction terms, sales-hat = 30 + 2.5 ad_spend + 8 promo, where promo = 1 in promotion weeks and 0 otherwise. What does the coefficient 8 mean?
choices: At the same advertising spend, promotion weeks average 8 thousand dollars more sales than non-promotion weeks
Sales increase by 8 thousand dollars for each additional promotion run
The advertising slope is 8 units steeper during promotions
8% of weeks had a promotion
questions.hint: An indicator compares its category with the baseline category.
questions.explanation: An indicator's coefficient is the estimated difference in average response between its category (promotion) and the baseline (no promotion), holding other predictors fixed. Without an interaction it shifts the intercept only; the slopes stay parallel.

cite.quote: the estimated difference in the average response between that category and the baseline category

questions.stem: A model codes store type with indicators for 'Mall' and 'Outlet'; 'Street' stores have both indicators equal to 0. The coefficient of Outlet is −4.2. Which comparison does −4.2 describe?
choices: Outlet stores versus Street stores
Outlet stores versus Mall stores
Outlet stores versus the average of all stores
Outlet stores versus stores with zero sales
questions.hint: Which category received no indicator?
questions.explanation: Street is the baseline category because it receives no indicator. Every indicator coefficient is a comparison with the baseline, so −4.2 compares Outlet with Street.

cite.quote: The category that receives no indicator is the baseline category

questions.stem: A fitted model is sales-hat = 39.863 + 2.479 ad_spend − 2.998 price + 11.134 promo + 0.992 ad_spend×promo. What is the slope of ad_spend in weeks with a promotion (promo = 1)?
questions.hint: With promo = 1 the interaction term becomes 0.992 × ad_spend.
questions.explanation: With promo = 1, ad_spend appears in two terms: 2.479 ad_spend + 0.992 ad_spend = 3.471 ad_spend. Reporting 2.479 gives the slope for non-promotion weeks only.

cite.quote: With a promotion the slope of ad_spend is 2.479 + 0.992 = 3.471

questions.stem: Using sales-hat = 39.863 + 2.479 ad_spend − 2.998 price + 11.134 promo + 0.992 ad_spend×promo, predict weekly sales (thousand dollars) for a store with ad_spend = 15, price = 12 and a promotion running.
questions.hint: The interaction variable equals ad_spend × promo = 15 × 1.

cite.quote: An interaction lets the slope of one predictor depend on the value of the other

questions.stem: In sales-hat = 39.863 + 2.479 ad_spend − 2.998 price + 11.134 promo + 0.992 ad_spend×promo, what is the estimated effect of running a promotion (in thousand dollars) for a store with ad_spend = 10?
questions.hint: Subtract the promo = 0 prediction from the promo = 1 prediction; most terms cancel.
questions.explanation: The promotion effect is 11.134 + 0.992 × ad_spend = 11.134 + 9.92 = 21.054. Because of the interaction, the effect is not the single number 11.134 — it grows with advertising spend.

cite.quote: The promotion effect is not a single number: it grows with advertising spend because of the interaction

questions.stem: The interaction term ad_spend×promo has a small p-value. Which statement follows?
choices: The relationship between advertising and sales has a different slope in promotion weeks than in other weeks
Advertising and promotion are strongly correlated with each other
Promotions have no effect on sales
The two lines for promotion and non-promotion weeks are parallel
questions.hint: An interaction is about slopes changing, not about predictors being correlated.
questions.explanation: A significant interaction means the slope of one predictor depends on the value of the other, so the two lines are not parallel. It says nothing about whether the predictors are correlated with each other.

cite.quote: An interaction lets the slope of one predictor depend on the value of the other

questions.stem: Weekly demand was 120, 132, 128, 140 and 136 units. Compute the three-week moving-average forecast for week 6 (to two decimals).
questions.hint: Average the three most recent values.
questions.explanation: (128 + 140 + 136)/3 = 404/3 = 134.67 units. Averaging all five weeks (131.2) uses the wrong window.

cite.quote: A moving-average forecast for the next period is the mean of the most recent k observations

questions.stem: With exponential smoothing and alpha = 0.3, the forecast for week 5 was 129.444 units and actual week-5 demand was 136 units. Compute the forecast for week 6.
questions.hint: New forecast = alpha × latest actual + (1 − alpha) × latest forecast.
questions.explanation: F(6) = 0.3(136) + 0.7(129.444) = 40.8 + 90.611 = 131.41 units. Swapping the weights (0.7 on the actual) gives 134.03, a common mistake.

cite.quote: F(t+1) = alpha Y(t) + (1 - alpha) F(t)

questions.stem: Demand for a product has just shifted to a permanently higher level. Which smoothing constant makes an exponential-smoothing forecast catch up fastest?
choices: alpha = 0.8
alpha = 0.5
alpha = 0.2
alpha = 0.05
questions.hint: Which value puts the most weight on the newest observation?
questions.explanation: A value of alpha close to 1 puts most of the weight on the latest observation, so the forecast responds quickly to a real change. Small values of alpha give smooth forecasts that respond slowly.

cite.quote: A value of alpha close to 1 puts most of the weight on the latest observation

questions.stem: Actual demand in four weeks was 132, 128, 140 and 136. The forecasts were 120, 123.6, 124.92 and 129.444. Compute the MAD (to two decimals).
questions.hint: Average the absolute values of the four errors.
questions.explanation: The errors are 12, 4.4, 15.08 and 6.556. Their absolute values sum to 38.036, so MAD = 38.036/4 = 9.51 units.

cite.quote: MAD, the mean absolute deviation, is the average of the absolute errors

questions.stem: A manager wants to compare forecast accuracy for a product sold in units and another sold in thousands of gallons. Which measure is most suitable?
choices: MAPE, because it expresses errors as percentages of actual values
MSE, because it is measured in squared units
MAD, because it uses the original units of each series
The sum of the forecast errors
questions.hint: Which measure does not depend on the units of the series?
questions.explanation: MAPE expresses absolute errors as percentages of the actual values, so it can be compared across series with different units. MAD and MSE are tied to each series' units, and raw errors cancel when summed.

cite.quote: so it can be compared across series with different units

questions.stem: A linear trend model gives a trend value of 250 units for next December. December's multiplicative seasonal index is 1.20. What is the seasonally adjusted forecast?
questions.hint: Multiply the trend value by the seasonal index.
questions.explanation: 250 × 1.20 = 300 units. An index of 1.20 means December typically runs 20% above trend. Adding 1.20 instead of multiplying confuses the multiplicative and additive models.

cite.quote: A seasonal index of 1.20 means the season is typically 20% above the trend
